newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks seen trading in tight range.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks seen trading in tight range.

text.p: Indian stocks are seen range-bound this week ahead of the Hindu new year with investors not enthused by falling interest rates and better first-half company results, brokers said at the weekend.
"I'm not bullish," said Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, member-broker at the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) and one of India's top individual taxpayers.
"I won't commit funds until I see a clear reversal."
The BSE's benchmark 30-share index fell 102.09 points, or 3.14 percent, to 3,148.57 last week despite better-than-expected results announced by top firms for the six months to September 30.

Most Indian banks cut their prime lending rates by 0.5-1.0 percentage point to 14.5-15.0 percent effective November 1 due to increasing liquidity. Yields on government securities and treasury bills also dropped by 50-75 basis points.
"The market discounts the future," said Jhunjhunwala. "The past is only a legacy."
He said the corporate results did not reflect a slowdown in industrial production, dwindling pace of new investment, infrastructural bottlenecks and tougher competition.
Other brokers said the market was likely to feel the pinch of selling by foreign institutional investors.
"The market is guided by (foreign institutional) selling and redemption demands for some domestic schemes," said Sanat Dalal, partner at BSE broking firm Sanat M. Dalal.
Trading this week will be restricted to four days up to Thursday because of the Festival of Lights, or Diwali, which heralds the Hindu new year for traders.
Traders said the possibility of a snap poll next year after national elections returned a fragile minority coalition in June was another reason for the weak undercurrent.
Some analysts say the market has discounted the mounting legal problems of former prime minister and former Congress party leader P.V. Narasimha Rao facing forgery and bribery charges.

"We don't expect the Congress party to withdraw support from the United Front government even if any of the cases against Mr Rao take an adverse turn," said brokerage firm Asit C. Mehta Investment Intermediates Ltd.
"In all probability, in such an eventuality, the Congress party would try and distance itself from Mr Rao to avoid further damage to the party's already sullied image," it said in a statement.
"The technical position...is down to sideways," it said. "We expect the market to be in the range of 3,200-2,950 points."
